subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does 'observational drawing' mean?
options: Drawing an object directly from looking at it in real life
Copying a drawing made by another artist
Drawing purely from memory without any reference
Tracing over a printed photograph
questions.explain: Observational drawing is made by looking directly at the actual subject rather than from memory or copies.

questions.q: Which mark-making technique uses closely spaced parallel lines to build up tone?
options: Hatching
Blending
Smudging
Washing
questions.explain: Hatching creates tone using sets of parallel lines placed close together.

questions.q: What is cross-hatching?
options: Overlapping sets of parallel lines that cross at angles
A single continuous unbroken outline
Small dots used to suggest tone
Rubbing graphite with a finger to soften it
questions.explain: Cross-hatching layers lines crossing at angles to build up darker, denser tone.

questions.q: The technique of building tone using many small dots is called what?
options: Stippling
Hatching
Scumbling
Contouring
questions.explain: Stippling uses a pattern of dots, with density controlling the depth of tone.

questions.q: What is a 'contour drawing'?
options: A drawing that focuses on the outlines and edges of a form
A drawing made only of solid blocks of tone
A quick scribble capturing movement
A drawing done entirely with dots
questions.explain: Contour drawing records the outline and internal edges of a subject with line.

questions.q: Why is 'blind contour drawing' a useful exercise?
options: It trains close looking by drawing without looking at the paper
It teaches you to shade smoothly and evenly
It helps you memorise perspective rules
It produces highly finished, accurate final pieces
questions.explain: Blind contour drawing sharpens observation because the artist watches the subject, not the page.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of 'gesture drawing'?
options: To capture the movement, pose and energy of a subject quickly
To produce a precise, detailed final rendering
To measure exact proportions with a ruler
To fill an area with even flat colour
questions.explain: Gesture drawing uses rapid, loose marks to record the essential movement and pose.

questions.q: You want to record the exact shape and details of a real seashell for your project. Which approach best fits observational drawing?
options: Draw it from life, looking carefully at the actual shell
Draw a shell from your imagination
Copy a cartoon shell from a comic
Trace a clip-art shell from the internet
questions.explain: Observational drawing means recording directly from the real object in front of you.

questions.q: In art, what does 'tone' refer to?
options: The lightness or darkness of an area
The type of line used
The overall colour of an object
The texture of a surface
questions.explain: Tone (or value) describes how light or dark something is, independent of its colour.

questions.q: The strong contrast between light and dark to create dramatic effect is known as what?
options: Chiaroscuro
Perspective
Foreshortening
Hatching
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro is the use of strong contrasts between light and dark to model form dramatically.

questions.q: What does 'form' describe in a drawing?
options: The three-dimensional, solid quality of an object
The flat outline of a shape only
The name of the artist's technique
The mood or feeling of the piece
questions.explain: Form is the illusion of three-dimensional volume, usually created through tone and shading.

questions.q: In linear perspective, what is a 'vanishing point'?
options: The point on the horizon where parallel lines appear to meet
The lightest highlight on an object
The centre of the composition
The darkest area of shadow
questions.explain: Receding parallel lines appear to converge at a vanishing point on the horizon line.

questions.q: In one-point perspective, how many vanishing points are used?
options: One
Two
Three
None
questions.explain: One-point perspective uses a single vanishing point, typical of a view looking straight down a road or corridor.

questions.q: The horizon line in a perspective drawing represents what?
options: The viewer's eye level
The brightest light source
The edge of the paper
The nearest object to the viewer
questions.explain: The horizon line corresponds to the viewer's eye level and is where vanishing points sit.

questions.q: What is 'foreshortening'?
options: When an object appears compressed because it recedes towards the viewer
When tone is applied evenly across a surface
When lines are drawn at exact right angles
When colours are made lighter in the distance
questions.explain: Foreshortening is the visual shortening of a form as it angles away from the viewer.

questions.q: You are drawing a cube seen from one of its corners, so two sides recede to opposite sides of the page. Which perspective are you using?
options: Two-point perspective
One-point perspective
Aerial perspective
No perspective
questions.explain: Viewing an object from a corner with two receding sides uses two vanishing points, i.e. two-point perspective.

questions.q: To make a circle on paper look like a solid, rounded sphere, what should you do?
options: Add graduated tone from light to dark across it
Draw a bold, even outline only
Fill it with a single flat grey
Add many small dots of equal spacing everywhere
questions.explain: Gradual tonal shading with highlights and shadows creates the illusion of three-dimensional form.

questions.q: What is a 'primary source' in art?
options: Something you observe and record first-hand yourself
An image copied from a book or website
A drawing given to you by a friend
A famous painting seen only in a textbook
questions.explain: Primary sources are gathered first-hand, such as your own photographs or drawings from life.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a 'secondary source'?
options: A photograph of an object taken from a magazine
A shell you draw from life
A still life you set up and observe
A landscape you sketch outdoors
questions.explain: Secondary sources are made by others, such as magazine images, books or internet photos.

questions.q: Why do artists annotate their sketchbook studies?
options: To explain their ideas, intentions and decisions in words
To make the page look more colourful
To fill empty space with random writing
To copy the exam board's mark scheme
questions.explain: Annotation records the artist's thinking, choices and evaluations alongside their visual work.
